title: Flip Every Binary Digit
statement:
Write the non-negative integer n in binary with no leading zeros. Turn every 0 into 1 and every 1 into 0, then read the result back as a number.

Return that number. The binary form of 0 is the single digit "0", so flipping it gives 1.

examples.why: 9 is 1001. Flipped it is 0110, which is 6. Only the four written digits flip, not the 28 leading zeros of a 32-bit int.
15 is 1111, all ones, so every digit becomes 0.
0 is written as one digit, "0", and it flips to 1.

hints: XOR with 1 flips a bit. Which bits should you flip?
Build a mask of all ones that is exactly as long as n's binary form.
Start with mask = 1 and keep doing mask = mask * 2 + 1 while mask < n. Then return mask XOR n.

explain.intuition:
Flipping a bit is XOR with 1. The only subtlety is which bits: just the ones that are written, from the highest 1-bit of n down to bit 0. A plain bitwise NOT (~n) would also flip all the leading zeros and give a negative number.

So build a mask of ones with the same length as n in binary, for 9 (1001) that is 1111, and XOR. Since n is at most the mask, mask − n gives the same answer.
pitfalls: Using ~n: it flips all 32 bits and returns a negative number.
Starting the mask at 0. Then n = 0 gives 0 instead of 1, because the one written digit never gets flipped.
Looping while mask <= n. For n = 15 that grows the mask to 31 and returns 16 instead of 0.

solutions.title: Flip digit by digit
solutions.idea: Peel off the lowest bit, flip it and put it in the same place in the answer. Do it at least once so 0 is handled.

solutions.title: All-ones mask and XOR
solutions.idea: Grow a mask of ones until it covers n, then XOR flips exactly the written digits.

followups: Do it in O(1) with a built-in that gives the bit length (or leading zero count) of n.
Flip only the bits between positions i and j of n.
